8.2.2 Cultural Resources Workers Environmental Awareness (WEAP) Training
Prior to the start of construction activities, all construction and managerial personnel shall undergo a
Cultural Resource Workers Environmental Awareness (WEAP) Training that will define and describe the
local cultural resources the crew may encounter, the role of the construction worker, the role of the
archaeological and tribal monitors in protecting the resources, and outline the relevant federal, state,
and local laws that apply to the project. The consulting Tribe[s] shall also have an opportunity to
contribute to the WEAP training. All workers must sign a form indicating completion of the WEAP
training.

8.2.3 Archaeological and Native American Monitoring
A qualified archaeologist and a Native American Monitor shall be retained to monitor all ground
disturbance associated with the proposed project. Ground disturbing activities include, but are not
limited to, demolition of the existing groin wall, new construction, and sand dredging. Within 90 days
of the conclusion of all monitoring activities, an archaeological monitoring report shall be prepared
and submitted to the appropriate local and federal agencies detailing the results of all monitoring
activities and any cultural resources identified. Any discoveries of cultural resources or human remains
must be addressed in accordance with the unanticipated discovery measures outlined below.

8.2.4 Unanticipated Discovery of Cultural Resources
Should archaeological resources (sites, features, or artifacts) be exposed during construction activities
for the proposed project, the monitors shall halt all construction work occurring within 100 feet of the
find until a qualified archaeologist, meeting the Secretary of the Interior’s Professional Qualification
Standards, can evaluate the significance of the find. Depending on the significance of the find, the
archaeologist may simply record the find and allow work to continue. In the event that an identified
cultural resource is of Native American origin, the qualified archaeologist will consult with the project
Applicant and the City of Avalon to implement Native American consultation procedures. If the
discovery proves significant under CEQA or Section 106 of the NHPA, additional work such as
preparation of an archaeological treatment plan, testing, or data recovery may be warranted.

8.2.5 Unanticipated Discovery of Human Remains
In accordance with Section 7050.5 of the California Health and Safety Code, if human remains are
found, the County Coroner shall be notified within 24 hours of the discovery. No further excavation or
disturbance of the site or any nearby area reasonably suspected to overlie adjacent remains shall occur
until the County Coroner has determined, within two working days of notification of the discovery, the
appropriate treatment and disposition of the human remains. If the remains are determined to be
Native American, the Coroner shall notify the NAHC in Sacramento within 24 hours. In accordance with
California Public Resources Code, Section 5097.98, the NAHC must immediately notify those persons
it believes to be the Most Likely Descendant (MLD) from the deceased Native American. The MLD shall

Dear Chairman Alvarez:

South Environmental was retained to conduct a cultural resources inventory for the proposed South
Beach Restoration Project (proposed project). The project site occupies an approximately 0.03-acre
area located at the shoreline near Crescent Avenue in Avalon on Santa Catalina Island. The project
site is located on the United States Geological Survey (USGS) Santa Catalina East, California 7.5-minute
Quadrangle Map in Section 27 of Township 09 South and Range 14 West (see enclosed Figure 1). The
project proposes to repair the South Beach seawall, the failed stairs, and potentially repair or replace
the stairs near the pier. The facilities are not to exceed the existing footprint. A like-for-like
reconstruction of a failed groin wall will also be done. Additionally, the project will dredge the sand
that has migrated from the beach into the harbor.

As part of the process of identifying potential cultural resources, South Environmental contacted the
Native American Heritage Commission (NAHC) and requested a Sacred Lands File search on May 3,
2024. The NAHC has not yet responded; however, we anticipate they will recommend we contact you
to seek comment.

If you have any knowledge of cultural resources that may exist within or near the project site, please
contact me at sjovanovic@southenvironmental.com or 562-900-8816, or via U.S. mail at the address
above.

Please note that the request herein is for informational purposes only and does not constitute
Assembly Bill 52 notification or initiation of consultation.

Respectfully submitted,

Historical Development of Avalon

Avalon began as an encampment called “Timm’s Landing” until George Shatto and Charles
Sumner purchased the island in 1887. That same year, the townsite was laid out and
renamed Avalon, with the Hotel Metropole being the first building constructed. In
addition to the construction of the first hotel on the island, Shatto also constructed
the first pier with the intention of turning the island into a tourist destination.

While Shatto’s financial situation did not allow his vision to come to fruition, in 1891,
William Banning purchased the island from Shatto. Following their purchase of the island,
he and his brothers formed the Santa Catalina Island Company in 1892. Once established
the Santa Catalina Island Company began to quickly develop Avalon and promote the new
resort concept. Contributions from the development company included an incline railway,
Buena Vista Park, aquarium, amphitheater, and glass bottom boat tours. The company also
provided transportation to the island. All of these developments contributed to the early
success of Avalon (Holder 1895; Pedersen 2006; Mallan 1984).

Avalon was officially incorporated as a city in 1913, but the initial success of the
City came to a halt when a massive fire destroyed much of the town in 1915. In the
aftermath of the fire, the Banning brothers attempted to rebuild, but the financial loss
was too substantial. In 1919, the brothers sold controlling interest in their company to
chewing gum magnate William Wrigley, Jr. Wrigley’s purchase set the stage for a new
period of development on the island that was on a much larger scale than previous efforts
(Holder 1895; Mallan 1984; Pedersen 2006; Guhan 2007).

Wrigley spared no expense on the promotion of the island and its redevelopment following
the fire. His contributions included the establishment of public utilities (e.g.
telephone service), several hotels, construction of the Catalina Country Club in 1921
and construction of the Catalina Casino in 1929. Wrigley also built the Island Villas to
replace the ever-growing tent city that was erected every summer when visitors arrived
on the island. These changes help to establish permanence on the island and led to
continued growth and development throughout the 20th Century (Holder 1895; Mallan 1984;
Pedersen 2006; Otte and Pedersen 2007).

When William passed away in 1932, his son Philip K. Wrigley continued and expanded his
father’s vision for the island. One of the key components of Philip’s plan for the island
was the re-design of Avalon. To assist him in this undertaking, he employed designers
Otis and Dorothy Shepherd (Otte and Pedersen 2007). The ambitious plan included the re-
design of Avalon, including the shoreline to enhance the visitor experience. The
aesthetic theme he chose was referred to as Early California. To achieve this concept,
Philip tasked the designers with everything from architectural styles, color palates,
plantings, streetscapes, marketing materials, and way finding systems (Guhan 2007, Otte
and Pedersen 2007). The development included several major construction and
infrastructure projects including the construction of the pedestrian walkway along
Crescent Avenue, construction of the seawall, construction of dams, and improvements in
public utilities (Mallan 1984; Otte and Pedersen 2007).

Following the onset of World War II, the island changed dramatically and was closed to
tourists after the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor. Following the closure of the island to
tourists, unused transport steamships were repurposed for use as military troop
transports. During this time several branches of the military began to utilize the island
as a training ground and operations location. United States military organizations that
used the island during this time included the Coast Guard, Army Signal Corps., Maritime
Service, and the Office of Strategic Services (later the CIA). The island was used until
the end of the war and at the time reopened to tourists (Otte and Pedersen 2007).

The next significant development in Avalon occurred in the late 1960s with the
construction of the Cabrillo Mole Terminal. Prior to the construction of the Terminal,
there were two piers on Avalon: the Pleasure Pier and the Steamer Pier. In the initial
plans from 1967, the intention was to remove both of the existing piers and replace them
with the new terminal (Anaheim Bulletin 1967) Despite public outcry, the Steam Pier was
demolished, but the Pleasure Pier was not (Press-Telegram 1969). The construction of the
Terminal allowed for more people to visit the island and also led to a redevelopment in
the area to support the new paths of circulation created by the Terminal and its
associated infrastructure.

During the mid-to-late twentieth century, the City of Avalon continued to grow with its
density and spread limited largely by the natural topography. Today the City has a
diverse historic built environment with Period Revival homes, vernacular cottages,
commercial buildings, and picturesque walkways along the water. Avalon remains the only
incorporated city on the island and provides many activities, dining, housing,
entertainment options, and continues to be a popular tourist destination.

Development of the South Beach Seawall

The Avalon Bay coastline served as the island’s commercial and tourism development center
from the 1880s through the present. The earliest development along the coast was
concentrated closer to the north end of the shoreline, near the Metropole Hotel, Bath

House, Tuna Club, and original Pleasure Pier. From the early 1900s, this northern
shoreline featured a concrete seawall and railings, that divided the beach and protected
the permanent buildings constructed on the land behind (Exhibit 1). The southern portion
was less developed, and primarily included a tent city along the sandy shoreline during
the tourist season (Exhibit 1). As this area continued to develop with more permanent
structures over the early decades of the 1900s, more robust shoreline development
occurred as well (Mallan 1984; Pedersen 2006; Otte and Pedersen 2007; Historic
Photographs Various; Sanborn Maps Various).

  Exhibit 1. Circa 1906 photograph of the Avalon Bay coastline showing denser
development and seawalls on the northern shoreline (foreground) and sparse development
  on the southern shoreline (Austin's Catalina Historical Archives (ACHA) 2024).

The stretch of beach now known as South Beach, running from the south side of the Green
Pleasure Pier towards the south before turning east, was originally undeveloped. In 1906-
1907, the South Beach section of the shoreline was developed with the “Freeholder Parallel
Pier”, initiated by the Banning Brothers. The pier was constructed of wood and ran
parallel to the shoreline, stretching from the original Steamer Pier and ending at the
shoreline south of the dancing pavilion. It was built to prevent unauthorized and non-
paying vessels from approaching the shore (Exhibit 2). A storm in 1908 severely damaged
the Freeholder Parallel Pier, and leftover lumber from it was used to construct the new
Pleasure Pier, now known as Green Pleasure Pier.

The Pleasure Pier (later known as Green Pleasure Pier) was constructed in 1908-1909.
Historic photographs of the pier near the time of its construction show that at this
time, there was no seawall along the South Beach shoreline (Exhibits 3 and 4). It appears

and the beach had been reverted to undeveloped land. The primary construction visible at
this time were several individual bench pavilions spaced evenly along the shore from
north to south. These appeared to include benches facing east and west, with small gable
roofs above to provide shade. In a photograph from 1914, the south end of the beach could
be seen as partially developed with a channel flanked by a wooden fence (Exhibit 3).
There appeared to be no visible concrete constructions or a seawall at this time.

By 1920, South Beach appeared to remain largely unchanged. A circa 1920 photograph of
beachgoers showed the undeveloped sandy beach, pavilions, and a rocky shoreline at the
south end of the beach where the coastline curved to the east (Exhibit 5). Another image
from 1928 of the Chicago Cubs baseball team warming up on South Beach shows the Green
Pleasure Pier in the background and no seawall (Exhibit 6).

Significance Evaluation

NRHP and CRHR Designation Criteria

The following presents an evaluation of the South Beach Seawall (subject property) in
consideration of NRHP and CRHR designation criteria.

NRHP Criterion A. That are associated with events that have made a significant
contribution to the broad patterns of our history.

CRHR Criterion 1. Is associated with events that have made a significant contribution to
the broad patterns of California’s history and cultural heritage.

The subject property was developed circa 1941 as part of the continuing evolution of the
city of Avalon. Following the fire in 1915, multiple infrastructure improvement projects
were undertaken on the island. Between 1915 and 1941, the Avalon Bay shoreline was
transformed to enhance the visitor and resident experience on the island. Before and
after the fire, development and infrastructure projects were focused on the areas to the

north and west of South Beach to support the considerably higher development happening
around the original Pleasure Pier, Bath House, Tuna Club, and later the casino. Even
after the construction of the Green Pleasure Pier in 1908-1909, the South Beach area
south of the new pier remained largely undeveloped, primarily serving as an untouched
beach adjacent to a tent city.

A review of historic photographs revealed that it was not until the 1940s that South
Beach underwent more significant development similar to what had been occurring to the
north for several decades. Starting in 1941, historic photographs show that the South
Beach Seawall began to be constructed in phases starting at the concrete channel on the
southeastern edge of the beach and continuing toward the pier. The first components
constructed appear to be the groin wall, the boat ramp, and one of the three staircases.
By 1962, the Seawall is extended to its current terminus and the staircases were added.

Given that the South Beach Seawall does not even begin to develop until circa 1941, this
is a very late infrastructure development project along Avalon Bay. Seawalls constructed
to the north of South Beach had been in place since the early 1900s, and the South Beach
Seawall only reached its current state circa by 1962, demonstrating its late development
period. While the South Beach Seawall development does generally coincide with more of
the permanent building developments on the southern portion of Avalon Bay’s shoreline
and bluffs, there is no archival evidence to suggest that the construction of the South
Beach Seawall was tied to any historical event or larger pattern of development. Further,
there is also no archival evidence to suggest that the design and construction of the
South Beach Seawall was connected to Philip Wrigley’s Avalon re-design project happening
in the 1930s that influences the design of other shoreline components in this part of
the City. Based on the timing of its construction and the overall development patterns
in the immediate area during these decades, the construction of the South Beach Seawall
appears to have been motivated by necessity and not a component of a larger planning
effort.

For these reasons, the subject property does not appear to be rise to the level of
significance required for designation. Therefore, the subject property is not eligible
under NRHP Criterion A or CRHR Criterion 1.

NRHP Criterion B. That are associated with the lives of persons significant in our past.

CRHR Criterion 2. Is associated with the lives of persons important in our past.

To be found eligible under B/2, a property must be directly tied to an important person
and the place where that individual conducted or produced the work for which he or she
is known. Archival research did not reveal any historical associations or connections to
specific people. Therefore, the subject property is not eligible under NRHP Criterion B
and CRHR Criterion 2.

NRHP Criterion C. That embody the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or

components may lack individual distinction.

possesses high artistic values.

The subject property was constructed between circa 1941 and circa 1962. It was designed
as a utilitarian structure and was constructed from poured concrete. Given its
utilitarian nature, there is no discernable architectural style and there appears to be
no innovative method of construction. Further, no architect or engineer was identified
throughout the course of archival research. For these reasons, there is nothing to
suggest that the subject property has the distinctive characteristics required for
designation. Therefore, the subject property is not eligible under NRHP Criterion C and
CRHR Criterion 3.

There is no evidence that the Seawall has the potential to yield information important to
national, state or local history. Therefore, it appears ineligible under NRHP Criterion D
and CRHR Criterion 4.

Integrity

Location: The subject property retains integrity of location. It is situated in its
original location.

Design: The subject property has a diminished integrity of design. There have been
multiple repairs to the original materials over the years that have diminished the
integrity of design.

Setting: The subject property no longer retains integrity of setting. While it remains
situated in the original location, the development associated with the Ferry terminal to
the east and north of the subject property has significantly altered its integrity of
setting. Further, the increased commercial development in the area makes this portion of
Avalon nearly unrecognizable compared to its appearance in the 1940s.

Materials: The subject property has a diminished integrity of materials. Much like its
integrity of design, the unsympathetic repairs made to the Seawall over time have
diminished the integrity of materials.

Workmanship: The subject property has a diminished integrity of workmanship. While it is
utilitarian in nature, deterioration and unsympathetic repairs have degraded the
integrity of the original workmanship.

Feeling: The subject property has no integrity of feeling. When it was constructed, the
area was much less developed along this quiet section of beach. With the development
surrounding the Seawall and the increased pedestrian traffic resulting from the
construction of the Ferry terminal, its integrity of feeling as a 1940s seawall on a
quiet beach has been compromised.

Association: No significant historical associations were identified as a result of
archival research.

DEPARTMENT ROLE

The Department is California’s Trustee Agency for fish and wildlife resources and holds
those resources in trust by statute for all the people of the state. (Fish & G. Code,
section 711.7, subd. (a) & 1802; Pub. Resources Code, section 21070; CEQA
Guidelines section 15386, subd. (a).) The Department, in its trustee capacity, has
jurisdiction over the conservation, protection, and management of fish, wildlife, native
plants, and habitat necessary for biologically sustainable populations of those species.
(Id., section 1802.) Similarly for purposes of CEQA, the Department is charged by law to
provide, as available, biological expertise during public agency environmental review
efforts, focusing specifically on projects and related activities that have the potential to
adversely affect fish and wildlife resources. The Department is also responsible for

PROJECT DESCRIPTION SUMMARY

Proponent: City of Avalon

Objective: The objective of the proposed Project is to address the erosive effects of
currents within Avalon Harbor and avoid future erosion of South Beach by constructing
groin wall/wingwall improvements, restoring 100 linear feet of the existing seawall,
repairing/enhancing existing shoreline access including the launch ramp and beach
access stairway surfaces, and replacing the beach sand with approximately 6,000 cubic
yards of imported sand.

Primary Project activities include the following:
  • Groin Wall Replacement: Construction activities include demolition of the
  current groin wall, the placement and interlocking of sheet piles into the bedrock
  using vibratory and/or impact hammer pile driving methods, installation of rebar
  or other reinforcement material and placement of concrete. The placement of
  sheet piles may involve pouring and curing concrete in the water if steel sheet
  piles with a concrete cap are used. Nearshore construction will take place by
  landside vehicles and machinery and there is a potential need for water vessels
  for offshore portions of the groin.
  • Seawall Restoration: Construction activities include restoring the majority of the
  eastern surface of the wall by repairing cracks and other defects and refinishing
  the surface. Approximately 80 feet of the seawall would be removed and
  replaced with a new section and access stairs. The new seawall will be placed
  using sheet piles that will be interlocked into the bedrock using vibratory and/or
  impact hammer pile driving methods. Construction will be completed by landside
  vehicles and machinery.
  • Launch Ramp and Stairway Restoration: Construction activities include
  repairing/restoring the surface of the existing launch ramp for small watercraft at
  the south end of the beach adjacent to the groin wall and the stairway down to
  the beach near the north end of South Beach.
  • Beach Nourishment: Construction activities include transporting sand via barge
  from the mainland to place approximately 6,000 cubic yards of sand to restore
  the beach surface. The barge will either directly travel to South Beach to offload
  the sand, or alternatively, the sand will be transported to the Avalon Freight
  Terminal and transported via truck to the beach (approximately 1 mile in
  distance) where it would be dumped from the shoreline access point and
  distributed around the beach using heavy equipment.

Location: The Project site is located at South Beach in the city of Avalon on Santa

segment of South Beach located between Green Pleasure Pier to the north and the

Timeframe: Construction of the proposed Project is anticipated to begin in early 2025

BIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE

Discussion and Comment: The Avalon Bay waters support many resident and
migratory fish and special status wildlife such as seabirds, marine mammals, and sea
turtles. The Avalon Bay waters also support commercially and recreationally important
fish and invertebrate species such as California halibut (Paralichthys californicus),
California spiny lobster (Panulirus interruptus), and Northern anchovy (Engraulis
mordax), which is an important forage fish.

COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The Department offers the comments and recommendations below to assist the City in
adequately identifying and/or mitigating the Project’s significant, or potentially
significant, direct, and indirect impacts on fish and wildlife resources.

I. Project Level Impacts and Other Considerations

Pile Driving and Sound Criteria

  Comments: The Project proposed to use large equipment for vibratory and pile
  driving methods for the installation of sheet pile during the groin wall replacement
  and seawall restoration activities. Underwater noise associated with pile driving
  activities may cause temporary or permanent impacts to fish, such as temporary
  movement out of the Project area, barotrauma injury, or mortality. The Department
  relies on guidance from the Fisheries Hydroacoustic Working Group to set safe
  sound pressure level (SPL) criteria for pile driving and pulling activities (Fisheries
  Hydroacoustic Working Group 2008, Attachment 1). The SPL dual criteria include a
  peak level of 206 dB and a cumulative sound exposure level (SEL) of 187 dB for fish
  2 grams and heavier or a cumulative SEL of 183 dB for fish less than 2 grams.
  Additionally, if hydraulic jetting or an impact hammer is used for pile driving, this may
  impact water quality, releasing contaminants from sediments into the water and/or
  creating turbidity that could harm marine life.

  Recommendations: The Department recommends that the MND include a model of
  the expected SPL and SELs for the Project’s casing drilling and/or pile driving  1.1
  activities. The Department appreciates the mitigation measures BIO-1, BIO-2, BIO-3,
  and BIO-4 that address some noise impacts to sensitive marine species. The

California Grunion

  Comments: California grunion (Leuresthes tenuis) leave the water at night to spawn
  on beaches during the spring and summer months. For four consecutive nights,
  beginning on the nights of the full and new moons, spawning occurs after high tides
  and continues for several hours. Spawning occurs from March 1st through August
  31st, and occasionally in February and September, with peak spawning in late March
  through June. Eggs are deposited during the highest tides of the month and incubate
  in the sand during the lower tides where they are kept moist by residual water in the
  sand. Eggs hatch after approximately 10-14 days, during the next hide tide series,
  when they are inundated by water and agitated by surf; however, eggs can remain
  viable for over a month in the sand. The Department is concerned that the Project’s
  beach nourishment/sediment placement construction activities may impact grunion
  spawning and hatching.

  Recommendation: The Department recommends all beach nourishment
  construction activities, including the use of heavy equipment, occur outside of the
  grunion spawning season (March 1st through August 31st). If avoiding the grunion
  spawning season is not feasible during sediment placement, the Department
  recommends that all activity related to sediment placement be restricted to above
  the kelp wrack line or the Higher High Water line from March 1st to August 31st.
  Furthermore, the locations of the spawning run should be marked physically and/or  1.6
  by Global Positioning System (GPS) locations. The density of the grunion throughout
  the area should be noted using the Walker Scale. The Project should ensure that
  maintenance workers avoid the spawning area and that a 50‐foot buffer is used to
  avoid impacting any spawning areas adjacent to the sediment placement sites. If
  grunion spawning occurs within the Project area, work in that area below the mean
  high tide line should not be conducted until after the grunion eggs have hatched (2
  weeks). The expected run schedule and further information about grunion can be
  found on CDFW’s website: https://wildlife.ca.gov/Fishing/Ocean/Grunion.

Marine Mammal and Sea Turtle Monitoring

  Comments: Harbor seals (Phoca vitulina), California sea lions (Zalophus
  californianus), other species of marine mammals, and sea turtles may be present or
  occur within the Project area. Construction activities, such as pile driving, within the
  Project area have the potential to impact these animals if they are present.

Invasive Species Impacts

  Comments: Disturbance of the bottom sediments from pile construction and
  anchoring may redistribute non-native species that compete with native species.
  This could cause widespread adverse impacts to eelgrass and marine ecology. The
  invasive alga Caulerpa taxifolia is listed as a federal noxious weed under the U.S.
  Plant Protection Act and while deemed eradicated in 2006 is monitored for potential
  future emergence. Another invasive alga species found recently in Newport Bay and
  San Diego Bay is Caulerpa prolifera, which is also a potential threat to growth and
  expansion of native eelgrass beds and other native algae. Caulerpa prolifera can
  grow as deep as 50 meters and appears to be more tolerant of low light
  environments than most other macroalgae. Additionally, since all Caulerpa species
  pose a serious risk in harming native marine life, Fish and Game Code Section 2300
  was amended in 2023 so that no person shall sell, possess, import, transport,
  transfer, release alive in the state, or give away without consideration all species of
  the genus Caulerpa, with the exception of bona fide scientific research upon
  authorization by the Department.

  Mr. Greenlaw:

  Coastal Commission staff appreciate the opportunity to review and comment on the Initial
  Study (IS) for the South Beach Restoration and Shoreline Access Enhancement Project
  (Project) related to the Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND). Given the potential for the
  project to be related to geological stability (coastal hazards), public access, water
  quality/biological resources, and Tribal Cultural Resources, as well as, potential
  implications for other ongoing projects nearby, additional and more thorough project review
  will be required as part of any necessary coastal development permit(s) (CDP) for the
  proposed project.

  The Project is within the Coastal Zone and constitutes development, so a coastal
  development permit(s) is required following the CEQA review period. A coastal
  development permit application was received to our office on September 18, 2024 and is
  currently under review. This letter is an overview of the main issues Commission staff has
  identified at this time based on the information that has been presented, and it is not an
  exhaustive analysis, nor a determination of the current CDP application being reviewed by
  Coastal Commission staff. The comments contained herein are preliminary in nature, and
  those of Coastal Commission staff only, and should not be construed as representing the
  official opinion of the Coastal Commissioners.

  While the City of Avalon has a certified Local Coastal Program (LCP), the development
  would occur partially within the Commission’s retained jurisdiction, as work would occur
  within open water and below the mean high tide line, and partially within the Commission’s
  appeal jurisdiction. Thus, the standard of review for this project is the Chapter Three
  policies of the Coastal Act, with the applicable policies of the City of Avalon LCP as
  guidance. The following are general comments on Coastal Act issues relevant to the
  Project.

  The stated purpose of the project is “to address the erosive effects of currents within
  Avalon Harbor” (page 3). The information provided identifies beach erosion of an
 approximately 300 linear ft. portion of South Beach between Green Pleasure Pier to the
north and the existing revetment along Pebbly Beach Road to the south as being primarily
linked to “failure of the existing groin wall/wingwall which extended from the seawall
adjacent to the launch ramp into Avalon Harbor” which “protected South Beach from
currents generated by passenger ferry boats docked at the mole ferry terminal
approximately 650 feet to the east, and by the impact of higher-horsepower ferries now
operating at the landing within the harbor.” The IS further states, “Over time, currents
generated by propeller/jet wash, which is directed westward to stabilize the boats when
docked, has pushed the beach sand into Avalon Harbor. This has exposed the subsurface
rock and impacted use of South Beach for recreational purposes. The intent of the project
is to replace the groin wall/wingwall to protect the beach from propellor/jet wash, restore
the seawall, launch ramp and beach access stairway surfaces and replace the beach sand
with approximately 8,000 cubic yards of imported sand.”

Pages 3 and 5 outline the four major components of the proposed project: 1) replacement
of the groin wall with a new approximately 18 in. wide, 60 ft. groin wall; 2) restoration of
approximately 80 linear ft. of an existing seawall which protects the upland promenade
east of Cresent Avenue; 3) the restoration and repair of an existing launch ramp and
stairway; and 4) replacement of approximately 6,000 c. y. of beach sand to restore beach
access.

While the California Coastal Commission (CCC) is not listed as a public agency from which
project approval is required (page 5), the project area does lie within the retained
jurisdiction of the CCC. To implement projects within the Coastal Zone, a coastal  2.1
development permit (CDP) from the Commission the City of Avalon must be found to
protect and enhance coastal resources, and consistent with policies of the Coastal Act.
Specifically, policies related to coastal hazards (Coastal Act Sections 30253, public access
(Coastal Act Sections 30210, 30211, 30212, and 30213), water quality/biological resources
(Coastal Act Sections 30230, 30231, 30233(a6), and 30235), and Tribal Consultation
which relate to the aforementioned project components.

Therefore, the following are Commission staff’s specific comments on the Project, broken
down by topic.

Coastal Hazards

The IS primarily reviews geologic stability for erosion, landslides, and seismic activity (VII.
Geology and Soils) but does not review sand placement in the context of source and
placement. The Project description includes a proposal for a one-time beach sand
placement/nourishment of between 6,000 c. y. and 8,000 c. y. (pages 3 and 5). The report  2.2
inconsistently sites both volume approximations for beach sand replenishment thus, it is
unclear which of these volumes is closest to the actual amount of sand required to
adequately address beach restoration. Additionally, there remain questions regarding the
source of the sand, the method of sand placement on the beach (hydraulic pipeline, truck
dump, etc.), donor site sand grain and toxicity analysis and grain size representative of the  2.3
receiver site. It is also unclear if the Project has been reviewed by the Southern California
Dredged Material Management Team and, if so, What the outcome was of that review. It
is also unclear if either of the proposed sand volumes, either 6,000 or 8,000 c. y., will be
sufficient to restore the entire beach envelope.
  2
 The Project proposal includes the construction of a new sheet-pile groin wall along the
eastern edge of South Beach. The IS states that the existing groin wall, which has failed, is
related to protection of the bay sediment “from currents generated by passenger ferry
boats” and from “impact of higher-horsepower ferries now operating in the landing within
the harbor.” Page 28 of the study states “The groin wall shows evidence of deterioration,
erosion, and spalling.” However, it is unclear as to when the wall failed, what caused the
failure, and if replacement and extension further bayward for a new groin wall would
sufficiently address sand erosion concerns. These details are important to assess in order 2.4
to determine how long the existing groin wall was functional and if the same factors that
lead to failure have changed over time or if the factors can be mitigated to maintain a new
groin wall. Updated information based on the currently proposed project that evaluates
current sand transport at the site (longshore transport rates, conceptual sand budget, etc.),
an alternatives analysis of different sand retention strategies (including different locations 2.5
for a groin/current deflector) and their tradeoffs, and an analysis on how the retention
strategies would be expected to influence downdrift sand supply is also needed.

The Project proposal includes the partial replacement of an approximately 80 ft. section of
an existing seawall. However, it is unclear if a seawall inspection report was generated to
  2.6
assess the portion of the wall proposed for repair or for the condition of the entire seawall.
It is also unclear as to if alternatives where analyzed that would still provide protection for
the public promenade and road while maximizing the amount of beach space.

It would also be helpful if an estimate of the annualized erosion rate of the backshore for
an unarmored condition and the fraction of the material behind the seawall that would
  2.7
contribute sand to the beach was also provided for analysis. Additionally, details as to how
much fill will be associated with all proposed project components including the proposed
groin wall are needed.

Public Access

Page 38 of the study states, “The proposed project would not require temporary lane
closures during construction as no work would occur on or proximal to a local street. Post
construction, the improvements will not affect emergency access; thus, the project will not
impact evacuation routes or otherwise impair evacuation during emergencies. A less than
significant impact would occur under this threshold.” However, page 14 of the study
estimates that sand replenishment alone would require “ a total of 400 one-way truck trips”
to “offload each barge” and that “These trips would occur on a different day than the
loading trips.” While there are no anticipated street closures, there remain questions as to 2.8
how construction access and staging will be addressed and if public access or recreation
will be impacted. Specifically, how will materials be stored and what routes will be taken by
any required machinery to access the site or is temporary fencing is proposed to be
placed? Coastal Act Sections 30210, 30211, 30212, and 30213 require that development
be sited and designed to avoid impacts to public access and low-cost recreational facilities.
Thus, it is important that information be provided regarding construction staging and
access to assess if there are anticipated access impacts to the sandy beach, public  2.9
walkways, and impacts to public views of the coast. Additionally, to fully assess access
impacts, an anticipated construction schedule beyond construction timing of “early to mid-
2025” is needed to clarify how and when access will be maintained or limited during
  3
 construction and if access will be restored or impacted following the conclusion of the
project.

Water Quality & Biological Resources

Section IV (Biological Resources) indicates that the proposed project may result in impacts
to special or sensitive species in the area or to species that could potentially use the area
for nesting/breeding habitat, including but not limited to, noise, light, vibration, and sand
placement impacts. While the information provided addresses impacts to views in the area
on page 9 (Aesthetics), the impact of lighting in a biological context remains unclear.

Pages 20-21 explains that the project site is within an area that could potentially serve as
habitat to special species including the green sea turtle, Western snowy plover, California
brown pelican, harbor seal, California sea lion, 14 fish species managed by the PFMC, and
topsmelt. While the Temporary Construction Noise and Temporary Water Quality Impacts
sections provide information on the potential impacts from vibration/pile driving, noise,
turbidity, and altered water chemistry without adequate mitigation measures and pages 23
and 24 include mitigation measures (BIO1 -BIO 7) which could potentially address impacts
  2.10
to sensitive species (e.g., retaining the services of “a qualified biological monitor”), a full
analysis of the mitigation measures that will ultimately be implemented for the project is
needed. Additionally, it is unclear whether the proposed development is the least
environmentally impactful alternative. A detailed explanation of all mitigation measures  2.11
proposed, and an alternatives analysis should be submitted for review.

Section IX (Hazards and Hazardous Materials) states that only fuel and petroleum
products will be used in the construction equipment and that fuel tanks will not be stored
on site. However, it is unclear exactly what materials and construction equipment are
needed for the project and what potential impacts to water quality, if any, are associated  2.12
with the materials and equipment. It would be helpful to understand all water quality Best
Management Practices (BMPs) that are proposed to be employed during construction
and/or to be incorporated into the project design and for all components of the Project.

Tribal Cultural Resources

Tribal government engage was noted as part of the initial study and while resources were
not found during the “intensive-level survey” staff recognize the importance of continued
engagement with tribal entities who have ancestral ties to the area, especially given that
the Gabrielino Tongva Indians of California, the Rincon Band of Luiseno Indians, and the
Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians have requested to consult with the lead agency and
have requested to have a tribal monitor present during all soil disturbing activities.
Additionally, the Rincon Band of Luiseno Indians, and the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash
Indians have requested consultation with the City of Avalon. Continued engagement and
the integration of the mitigation measures such as those outlined on page 30 and that align
with the Commission’s 2018 Adopted Tribal Consultation Policy are encouraged. To  2.13
ensure that tribal cultural, archeological, and paleontological resources are protected,
analysis of which mitigation measures will be implemented as part of the proposed project
is needed.

  4
 Please note that the comments provided herein are preliminary in nature. More specific
comments may be appropriate as the project develops. Coastal Commission staff requests
notification of any future activity associated with this project or related projects. Thank you
for the opportunity to comment on the Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) for the Avalon
Harbor Club Dock Replacement Project (Project). Please contact me at Elishebah.Tate-
Pulliam@Coastal.ca.gov with any questions.

improvements, repair/enhance existing shoreline access, and replace beach sand (“Project”) along
the southeast shoreline of Avalon Harbor, known as South Beach, located between Green Pleasure
Pier to the north and the existing revetment along Pebbly Beach Road to the south, a distance of
approximately 300 linear feet (“Site”); and

  WHEREAS, South Beach is a primary point of public access for residents and visitors to
coastal recreation resources within the city; and

  WHEREAS, the Planning Commission has authority per Avalon Municipal Code (AMC)
Sections 9-8.203.a to review and take action on the subject applications for a Site Plan and
associated environmental determination; and

  WHEREAS, the Site is categorized Resort Recreation – High Density by the General Plan
Land Use Element and is located within the Resort Recreation (R/R) zoning district; and

  WHEREAS, the Site is located within the Coastal Zone and is subject to processing of a
consolidated Coastal Development Permit by the California Coastal Commission; and

  WHEREAS, pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources
Code, § 21000 et seq.) and the State CEQA Guidelines (California Code of Regulations, title 14,
§ 15000 et seq.) (Collectively, “CEQA”), the City is the lead agency for the proposed Project; and

an Initial Study to analyze whether the proposed Project may cause a potentially significant effect
on the environment; and

  WHEREAS, based on the information contained in the Initial Study, which concluded that
the proposed project could have potentially significant impacts but that those impacts could be
reduced to less than significant levels with implementation of proposed mitigation measures, the
City determined that a Mitigated Negative Declaration should be prepared for the proposed
Project, and the IS/MND (State Clearinghouse (SCH) No. 2024101329) was prepared pursuant to
CEQA; and

   WHEREAS, pursuant to Public Resources Code section 26081.6 and State CEQA

(“MMRP”) for reporting on or monitoring the changes which it has either required in the proposed

review and comment period beginning on October 29, 2024, and with the public review period

SECTION 1 – ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

COMPLIANCE WITH THE CALIFORNIA ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ACT. The
Planning Commission has reviewed and considered the information contained in the IS/MND,
comments received, and other documents contained in the administrative record for the Project.
Based on the Planning Commission’s independent review and analysis, the Planning Commission
finds that the IS/MND and administrative record contain a complete and accurate reporting of the
environmental impacts associated with the proposed Project, and that the IS/MND has been
completed in compliance with CEQA and the State CEQA Guidelines.
FINDINGS ON ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS. Based on the whole record before it, the
Planning Commission finds and determines that evidence in the administrative record, including,
without limitation, the analysis and conclusions set forth in the staff report, responses to comments,
testimony provided at the proposed Project’s public hearing, the IS/MND and the supporting
technical studies, demonstrate that, with incorporation of the identified mitigation as set forth in
the Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP), the proposed Project will not have

  2
 any potential significant environmental impacts. The Planning Commission further finds and
determines that there is no substantial evidence in the administrative record supporting a fair
argument that the proposed Project may have a significant environmental impact. The Planning
Commission finds that the IS/MND contains a complete, objective, and accurate reporting of the
environmental impacts associated with the proposed Project and reflects the independent judgment
and analysis of the City.
SECTION 2 – FINDINGS

General Plan/Local Coastal Plan Consistency

The Resort Recreation (R/R) zoning designation of the Project site is consistent with the General
Plan land use designation of Resort Recreational – High Density (RR-HD).

The proposed Project implements the following General Plan Goals and Policies:

Policy II-16 of the Land Use Element:

  “Provide an interconnected network of open spaces, active and passive parks, and resort
  recreational amenities with an emphasis on pedestrian access.”

Policy III-5 of the Open Space Element:

  “Provide an open space and recreation system with an appropriate balance of facilities
  suitable for intensive use (beaches, playgrounds, sports fields) and those suitable for low
  intensity use (hiking, camping, golf) that meets the needs of residents and visitors.”

  Open space is a key component of the City’s character, representing a scenic resource of
  great value and importance to the quality of life for Avalon residents and visitors. The RR-
  HD designation accommodates a variety of uses associated with the resort character of
  Avalon, including public recreational access to Avalon Bay. The proposed project will
  restore beach sand along South Beach and repair the existing stairwell and launch ramp,
  which will enhance the public’s access to recreational opportunities in a heavily-utilized
  area of the city.

Site Plan Review

The proposed Project requires approval of a Site Plan per AMC Section 9-8.201. AMC Section 9-
8.203 sets forth the required findings for approval of a Site Plan Review as follows:

  1. Every use, development of land and application of development standards shall take place
  in compliance with all applicable provisions of this title. (AMC Section 9-8.203.a)

  The R/R zone is established for the purpose of stimulating and allowing a variety of uses
  associated with the resort character of Avalon. The proposed project consists of restoration
  and enhancement of existing beach and public recreational facilities, which are not subject
  to issuance of a new conditional use permit. The proposed project complies with the
  development standards for structures adjacent to the mean high tide line as set forth in

  3
   AMC Section 9-6.404.c. The project consists erosion control and maintenance projects, as
  well as visitor serving recreation access facilities, including repair of access stairs and a
  boat launch ramp, which do not obstruct views to Avalon Bay from Crescent Avenue.

  2. Every use, development of land and application of development standards shall be
  considered on the basis of the suitability of the site for the particular use or development
  intended, and the total development, including the application of prescribed development
  standards, shall be so arranged as to avoid traffic congestion, insure the protection of
  public health, safety and general welfare, prevent adverse effects on neighboring property
  and shall be in general accord with all elements of the General Plan. (AMC Section 9-
  8.203.b)

  The proposed project is designed to fit within the density and scale of development along
  the public beachfront along Avalon Bay. Existing development in the immediate area
  includes public recreational facilities and commercial retail, restaurant, and hotel
  accommodations. Restoration of beach sand and repair and replacement of recreational
  amenities will continue to sit within the intended uses permitted within the R/R zone and
  contemplated in RR-HD General Plan land use designation, and will not have an adverse
  effect on neighboring properties.

  The project site is located seaward of Crescent Avenue. This is a heavily traveled area by
  both vehicles and pedestrians and identified as Major Circulation Facilities in the General
  Plan Circulation Element. There have been no reported traffic issues associated with the
  existing recreational facilities, and it is anticipated that existing infrastructure will ensure
  that traffic associated with visitor and resident use of the area will not interfere with
  circulation along Crescent Avenue.

  3. Every use, development of land, application of development standards shall be considered
  on the basis of suitable and functional development design, but is not intended that such
  approval be interpreted to require a particular style or type of architecture. (AMC Section
  9-8.203.c)

  The project site is located within a developed area of Avalon, on public property with
  coastal frontage along Avalon Bay. The design elements in the proposed plans are
  consistent with the established scale of development adjacent to the mean high tide line
  and not stand out as inconsistent with existing development on the site or in the vicinity.

Coastal Development Permit

The City of Avalon is located entirely within the Coastal Zone. The Avalon Local Coastal Program
(LCP) was adopted in 1981 (amended 1993) to guide the management and development of the
city’s unique coastal resources. The LCP grants the City Planning Commission authority to review
and grant Coastal Development Permits (CDPs) for all qualifying development projects within the
boundaries of the LCP, including coastal areas landward of the mean high tide line (MHTL). The
California Coastal Commission retains jurisdiction for granting CDPs for all projects seaward of
the MHTL.

  4
 The Project site includes lands that are both landward and seaward of the MHTL into the waters
of Avalon Bay. Since the project site spans both the City and Coastal Commission’s jurisdictions,
the City has opted to defer authority to process a consolidated CDP directly to the Coastal
Commission.

Condition #3 of the draft resolution states that the Coastal Commission shall have final authority
to process and approve the CDP for the Project, and that all conditions of approval of the CDP
shall be incorporated into the Planning Commission approval of the Project.

Annual Growth Policy

The growth policy provides that new development will only be permitted with confirmation from
Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) that adequate fresh water is available. The project
does not include potable water as part of its operation and is therefore not subject to evaluation of
an allocation for water service. The project will also not have growth inducing effects, as it
involves modification and enhancement of existing public recreational facilities. Staff
recommends that the Planning Commission make the finding that the proposed project is in
compliance with the 2025 Annual Growth Policy.

  8.103.d.1)

  Determination of conformance for projects within the City of Avalon includes analysis of
  whether the proposed project conforms with the Avalon General Plan, the Local Coastal
  Plan for Avalon, as well as the Avalon Zoning and Affordable Housing Ordinances, as
  applicable.

  •  General Plan/Local Coastal Plan: The Low Density Residential (LD) zoning
  designation of the project site is consistent with the General Plan land use designation
  of Low Density Residential.

  7
   The proposed project implements the following General Plan Goals and Policies:

  Policies II-20 and II-21 of the Land Use Element:

  “Pursue new developments and businesses that add to the City’s economic base,
  particularly those that general sales tax and transient occupancy tax.”

  “Expand lodging choices by attracting and retaining desirable and high-quality
  facilities to the community.”

  The City recognizes that short-term rentals contribute significantly to economic
  development. allow visitors to experience the unique island community of Avalon, and
  assist in providing access to the coast. Permitting and regulation of short-term rentals
  through the Transient Rental License process allows the City to monitor rental activity
  to ensure their operation has minimal negative impact to surrounding properties and
  also provides a significant income from transient occupancy tax, which is paid monthly
  to the City.

  provides access to alternative forms of accommodation for visitors to the community
  within existing developed properties, supplementing the need for new visitor-serving
  development. Continued permitting and management of short-term rentals in the
  community is consistent with the intent of the LCP and implements Sections 30213 and
  30222 of the California Coastal Act.

Annual Growth Policy
The growth policy provides that new residential or commercial development should only be

SUMMARY: A Public Hearing considering a Transient Rental License and Coastal Development
Permit to allow renting or leasing of a room or rooms for periods of fewer than thirty (30)
consecutive days duration in the Low Density Residential (LD) zone at 46 Playa Azul. The
Proposed Project is categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
per State CEQA Guidelines 15301 (Class 1 - Existing Facilities). The proposed project is located
within the appealable area of the Coastal Zone.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):

  1. Conduct a public hearing;

  2. Find this project exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant
  to Section 15301 under Class 1 (Existing Facilities) of the CEQA Guidelines, because it
  has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment; and

  3. Adopt Resolution No. PC 25-53 approving a Transient Rental License and Coastal
  Development Permit pursuant to PC#2891 (Attachment 1).

AUTHORIZING GUIDELINES: Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Sections 3-1.309 and 9-8.103.a
authorize the Planning Commission to review and take action on applications for a Transient

Existing Site and Area Context:

The project site is located within a thirteen-unit condominium building within the Hamilton Cove
development. The building is situated between Gaviota to the north and Playa Azul to the south.
The lot slopes dramatically to the southeast towards Hamilton Cove.

The unit is located on the fourth level of the building, located on the same level as two other
units, 45 and 47 Playa Azul. All three units share an interconnected balcony. Originally
constructed in 1991, the residence has not been significantly modified since it was completed.

All abutting properties are in the LD zone and represent a mix of single-family residential villas
and residential condominiums within Hamilton Cove. A vicinity map, including adjacent property
types and existing short-term rental status, is provided as Attachment 2 of this report.

Entitlement and Permit History:

The project site has not been granted any previous entitlements.

There are no active or recent building permits for this property.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION: The applicant, Damien Salerno, proposes to short-term rent a two
bedroom, two bathroom single-family condominium unit. The residence is on a single level, with
interior living space and a shared balcony. The entire residence will be rented as a single unit.
The residence is approximately 1,403 square feet in size. The maximum occupancy of the unit
will be six (6) individuals based on the bedroom count and license limitations set forth in AMC
Section 3-1.317.g.

The transient rental application and proposed rental floor plan are included in Attachments 3
and 4 of this report.

It is the opinion of Staff that existing regulations and standard conditions adequately address
potential nuisance concerns related to transient rental, and no additional conditions are required

The City of Avalon is located entirely within the Coastal Zone. The project is located within the

of use that requires issuance a Coastal Development Permit per AMC Section 9-8.102.b.2.v, on
the following findings:

  1. The use is in conformance with the certified Local Coastal Program. (AMC 9-
  8.103.d.1)

  Determination of conformance for projects within the City of Avalon includes analysis of
  whether the proposed project conforms with the Avalon General Plan, the Local Coastal
  Plan for Avalon, as well as the Avalon Zoning and Affordable Housing Ordinances, as
  applicable.

  •  General Plan/Local Coastal Plan: The Low Density Residential (LD) zoning
  designation of the project site is consistent with the General Plan land use designation
  of Low Density Residential.

  The proposed project implements the following General Plan Goals and Policies:

  Policies II-20 and II-21 of the Land Use Element:

  “Pursue new developments and businesses that add to the City’s economic base,
  particularly those that general sales tax and transient occupancy tax.”

  “Expand lodging choices by attracting and retaining desirable and high-quality facilities
  to the community.”

  The City recognizes that short-term rentals contribute significantly to economic
  development and allow visitors to experience the unique island community of Avalon
  and assist in providing access to the coast. Permitting and regulation of short-term
  rentals through the Transient Rental License process allows the City to monitor rental
  activity to ensure their operation has minimal negative impact to surrounding
  properties and also provides a significant income from transient occupancy tax, which
  is paid monthly to the City.

  •  Avalon Local Coastal Program (LCP): The Avalon Local Coastal Program (LCP)
  emphasizes the fact that Avalon is a visitor-focused community, with multiple visitor-
  serving facilities and recreational opportunities. Availability of short-term rentals
  provides access to alternative forms of accommodation for visitors to the community
  within existing developed properties, supplementing the need for new visitor-serving
  development. Continued permitting and management of short-term rentals in the
  community is consistent with the intent of the LCP and implements Sections 30213
  and 30222 of the California Coastal Act.

Annual Growth Policy
The growth policy provides that new residential or commercial development should only be
permitted with confirmation from Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) that adequate
fresh water is available. The project involves permitting short-term rental use of an existing
residential unit, with no modifications to the floor plan or bedroom count. Water demand for
residential buildings is calculated based on the number of bedrooms in the unit. Since the floor
plan of the unit is not impacted, the project is not subject to evaluation of an allocation for water
service. Therefore, staff recommends that the Planning Commission make the finding that the
proposed project is in compliance with the 2025 Annual Growth Policy.

ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION: The proposed project is categorically exempt from the
provisions of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines
15301 (Class 1 – Existing Facilities) because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the
environment.

The Class 1 exemption includes the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing,

Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15301 (Class 1 – Existing Facilities) because it
has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.
The Class 1 exemption includes the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing, licensing,
or minor alteration of existing public or private structures, facilities, mechanical equipment, or
topographical features, involving negligible or no expansion of use. The project involves
permitting short-term rental use for an existing residential unit, involving no expansion of the

 residential use on the project site, in compliance with all operational regulations set for in Avalon
Municipal Code Chapter 3-1, Business Licensing, Article 3, Transient Rental Licenses. As such,
the project is not expected to have a significant environmental impact on the surrounding area.
Furthermore, the project was evaluated pursuant to the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions
as identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and the
Planning Commission finds that there are no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the project.

The proposed project may be granted a Transient Rental License for short-term rental per AMC

  materially detrimental to the property of other persons located in the vicinity of such use.

  Standard conditions of approval for all transient rentals as set forth in AMC Section 3-
  1.317 have been incorporated into the approval of the project. No additional special
  conditions are required in order to ensure compliance with the transient rental license
  operational regulations.

  b) In making such determination, the Planning Commission shall find that the proposed
  transient rental use is in general accord with the following principles and standards:

  1)  The nature, condition, and development of adjacent uses, buildings and structures
  shall be considered and no proposed transient rental use shall be permitted where
  such use will adversely affect or be materially detrimental to said adjacent uses,
  buildings and structures;

  The subject property is an existing single-family condominium unit located within
  a multi-unit building in Hamilton Cove. No modifications to the property are
  proposed that would alter the ability of the building to function as a single-family
  condominium residence in the future. The property was inspected by the Planning
  and Building Department prior to the public hearing and no health and safety issues
  were identified by the inspector that would prevent the residence from being used

  2
   as a transient rental. Standard conditions of approval ensure that operation of the
  transient rental will remain orderly and not have an adverse effect on surrounding
  residential properties.

2)  The site for a proposed transient rental use shall be adequate in size and shape to
  accommodate the yards, walls, fences, parking and loading facilities, landscaping,
  outdoor entertaining areas and other development features prescribed in this
  chapter or as required as a condition in order to integrate said use and not be
  detrimental with the uses in the neighborhood;

  The subject property is an existing two bedroom, two bathroom single-family
  condominium unit. The residence includes kitchen, indoor living area, and exterior
  deck which will all be accessible to transient guests. The property will offer a
  vehicle for transient rental guests, which has a designated off-street parking space.

3)  The site for a proposed transient rental use shall be served by highways and streets

  The project site is located between Gaviota and La Playa Azul within the Hamilton

Coastal Development Permit
The City of Avalon is located entirely within the Coastal Zone. The project is located within the
300-foot appealable boundary of the Coastal Zone and qualifies as an increase in the intensity of
use that requires issuance a Coastal Development Permit per AMC Section 9-8.102.b.2.v, on the
following findings:
  1. The use is in conformance with the certified Local Coastal Program. (AMC 9-
  8.103.d.1)

  Determination of conformance for projects within the City of Avalon includes analysis of
  whether the proposed project conforms with the Avalon General Plan, the Local Coastal
  Plan for Avalon, as well as the Avalon Zoning and Affordable Housing Ordinances, as
  applicable.

  7
   •  General Plan/Local Coastal Plan: The Low Density Residential (LD) zoning
  designation of the project site is consistent with the General Plan land use designation
  of Low Density Residential.

  The proposed project implements the following General Plan Goals and Policies:

  Policies II-20 and II-21 of the Land Use Element:

  “Pursue new developments and businesses that add to the City’s economic base,
  particularly those that general sales tax and transient occupancy tax.”

  “Expand lodging choices by attracting and retaining desirable and high-quality
  facilities to the community.”

  The City recognizes that short-term rentals contribute significantly to economic
  development and allow visitors to experience the unique island community of Avalon
  and assist in providing access to the coast. Permitting and regulation of short-term
  rentals through the Transient Rental License process allows the City to monitor rental
  activity to ensure their operation has minimal negative impact to surrounding properties
  and also provides a significant income from transient occupancy tax, which is paid
  monthly to the City.

  •  Avalon Local Coastal Program (LCP): The Avalon Local Coastal Program (LCP)
  emphasizes the fact that Avalon is a visitor-focused community, with multiple visitor-
  serving facilities and recreational opportunities. Availability of short-term rentals
  provides access to alternative forms of accommodation for visitors to the community
  within existing developed properties, supplementing the need for new visitor-serving
  development. Continued permitting and management of short-term rentals in the
  community is consistent with the intent of the LCP and implements Sections 30213 and
  30222 of the California Coastal Act.

  •  LD Zone Development Standards: The proposed project does not involve any
  modifications or additions to an existing building that require analysis pursuant to the
  development standards for the LD zone. No adjustments or variances are required to
  permit the proposed project.

  •  Affordable Housing Ordinance: This ordinance is not applicable to the proposed project
  since the proposal does not include the development of five or more residential units.

2. For all development seaward of the nearest public highway to the shoreline, the
  proposed development conforms to the public access and recreation policies of
  Chapter 3 of the Coastal Act. (AMC 9-8.103.d.2)

  8
   The project site is not seaward of Gaviota, which is the nearest roadway access to the
  shoreline relative to the location of the project site. The proposed project involves
  permitting short-term rental use of an existing developed residential property in a
  residential area of the city, in compliance with development standards for the LD zone and
  Transient Rental License regulations. Therefore, the project does not involve a change in
  land use, density, or intensity that will result in increased demand for public access and
  recreation opportunities. Furthermore, the project does not include any building or site
  modification that could block or impede existing public access opportunities.
Annual Growth Policy
The growth policy provides that new residential or commercial development should only be
permitted with confirmation from Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) that adequate
fresh water is available. The project involves permitting short-term rental use of an existing
residential unit, with no modifications to the floor plan or bedroom count. Water demand for
residential buildings is calculated based on the number of bedrooms in the unit. Since the floor
plan of the unit is not impacted, the project is not subject to evaluation of an allocation for water
service. Therefore, staff recommends that the Planning Commission make the finding that the
proposed project is in compliance with the 2025 Annual Growth Policy.

Permit to allow renting or leasing of a room or rooms for periods of fewer than thirty (30)
consecutive days duration in the Low Density Residential (LD) zone at 204 Mar de Cortez. The
Proposed Project is categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
per State CEQA Guidelines 15301 (Class 1 - Existing Facilities). The proposed project is not
located within the appealable area of the Coastal Zone.

  1. Conduct a public hearing;

  2. Find this project exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant
  to Section 15301 under Class 1 (Existing Facilities) of the CEQA Guidelines, because it

authorize the Planning Commission to review and take action on applications for a Transient

Existing Site and Area Context:

The project site is located on a regularly shaped parcel addressed 204 Mar de Cortez. The parcel
is situated between Mar de Cortez to the north and La Paloma to the south. The lot slopes
dramatically to the southeast towards the coastline.

The project site is currently developed with a four-story residence with three exterior decks facing
the coastline. Originally constructed in 2021, the residence has not been significantly modified
since it was completed.

All abutting properties are in the LD zone and represent a mix of single-family residential villas
and residential condominiums within Hamilton Cove. A vicinity map, including adjacent property
types and existing short-term rental status, is provided as Attachment 2 of this report.

Entitlement and Permit History:

The project site has not been granted any previous entitlements.

There are no active or recent building permits for this property.
   PC#2889 – 204 Mar de Cortez
  Page 3

PROJECT DESCRIPTION: The applicant, Les Blake, proposes to short-term rent a seven
bedroom, eight bathroom single-family residence. The residence is four levels, with two kitchens,
three outdoor decks, a game room, and a personal theater. The entire residence will be rented
as a single unit. The residence is approximately 7,457 square feet in size. The maximum
occupancy of the unit will be sixteen (16) individuals based on the bedroom count and license
limitations set forth in AMC Section 3-1.317.g.

The transient rental application and proposed rental floor plan are included in Attachments 3
and 4 of this report.

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS: Staff has identified two issue items for discussion regarding the
proposed project related to the use of the exterior decks.

Issue 1: Exterior Decks

The subject property has three exterior decks that will be accessible to transient renters. Exterior
decks are common within the Hamilton Cove development, as units are designed to take
advantage of the sweeping views of the coastline in the area. Nuisance noise is generally a
concern for residents of any residential area. The villas area of Hamilton Cove is not as densely
developed as the condominium area, but there is potential for sound to travel due to the
geography of the development.

The property is located within Noise District 2. This is the district assignment for commercial
areas or other areas not depicted on AMC Section 5-13.04 Table 2. AMC Section 5-13.08.a.2.a
prohibits the operation of sound amplifying equipment outdoors in such a manner as to be plainly
audible from the real property line of which the sound amplifying equipment is located, absent
approval of a Special Use Permit.

AMC 3-1.317 provides standard conditions which are applicable to all transient rental and
incorporated into the draft resolution. Two conditions prohibit the use of unenclosed balconies
and patios between the hours of 9:00 PM and 8:00 AM (Condition #8) and also require that all
transient rentals comply with the noise regulations set for in AMC Chapter 5-13, Noise (Condition
#9).

Therefore, it is the opinion of Staff that existing regulations and standard conditions adequately
address potential nuisance noise concerns related to the exterior decks and no additional
conditions are required to meet the findings required to grant a TRL for the property.

Issue 2: Maximum Rental Occupancy

The maximum occupancy of the unit will be sixteen (16) individuals based on the bedroom count
and license limitations set forth in AMC Section 3-1.317.g., which is two individuals per bedroom
plus two additional persons. This is a large number of people compared to the standard single-
family residence. However, the residence itself is over 7,000 square feet in size and includes a
large number of interior living areas and amenities that are not otherwise found in other
neighborhoods within the city. Therefore, staff does not recommend any additional conditions
further limiting the maximum occupancy of the transient rental.

However, pursuant to standard Condition #7 of the draft resolution, the Planning Commission
may establish a different maximum occupancy number. This may be done when appropriate and

reasonable, for example, when justified by unique site characteristics of the property. Reasons
for establishing a different maximum occupancy number include, but are not limited to:

  a. Size and location of the property;
  b. Distinction between single- and multi-unit properties; and
  c. Number and size of each sleeping room in the transient rental unit

licensing, or minor alteration of existing public or private structures, facilities, mechanical
equipment, or topographical features, involving negligible or no expansion of use. The project
involves permitting short-term rental use for an existing residential unit, involving no expansion

Avalon Municipal Code Chapter 3-1, Business Licensing, Article 3, Transient Rental Licenses.
As such, the project is not expected to have a significant environmental impact on the

SECTION 1 – ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

The proposed project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15301 (Class 1 – Existing Facilities) because it
has no potential to have a significant effect on the environment.
The Class 1 exemption includes the operation, repair, maintenance, permitting, leasing, licensing,
or minor alteration of existing public or private structures, facilities, mechanical equipment, or
topographical features, involving negligible or no expansion of use. The project involves

  1
 permitting short-term rental use for an existing residential unit, involving no expansion of the
residential use on the project site, in compliance with all operational regulations set for in Avalon
Municipal Code Chapter 3-1, Business Licensing, Article 3, Transient Rental Licenses. As such,
the project is not expected to have a significant environmental impact on the surrounding area.
Furthermore, the project was evaluated pursuant to the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions
as identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and the
Planning Commission finds that there are no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the project.
The project does not impact an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern, does not
result in cumulative impacts, does not have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual
circumstances, does not damage scenic resources within a state scenic highway, is not a hazardous
waste site, and is not identified as a historical resource.

  area of Hamilton Cove. No modifications to the property are proposed that would

  The property was inspected by the Planning and Building Department prior to the
  public hearing and no health and safety issues were identified by the inspector that
